Name: cv_construction_drawing_survey
Title: Computer Vision for Construction Drawing Understanding: A Comprehensive Survey
Short Hypothesis: Despite significant advances in applying computer vision to construction drawings — including floor plans, structural drawings, MEP diagrams, and P&IDs — no unified survey exists that systematically covers CV methods across all construction drawing types, leaving researchers without a coherent map of the field's progress, gaps, and opportunities.
Related Work: Existing surveys address only narrow slices of construction drawing analysis. Dodge et al. (2017) and Zeng et al. (2019) focus exclusively on architectural floor plan recognition. Lu et al. (2019) and Paliwal et al. (2021) survey methods for P&ID digitization but ignore other drawing types. Broader surveys on Visual Rich Document (VRD) understanding (e.g., Huang et al. 2022, Borchmann et al. 2021) cover invoices, forms, and receipts but treat construction drawings as a peripheral concern. Zhao et al. (2023) survey document layout analysis without addressing the unique challenges of technical drawings such as sparse line art, domain-specific symbols, and multi-scale objects at 10K+ pixel resolutions. Recent foundation model surveys (Kirillov et al. 2023 on SAM, Li et al. 2023 on Grounding DINO) demonstrate strong zero-shot capabilities on natural images but do not evaluate performance on engineering drawings. Our survey distinguishes itself by providing the first comprehensive, cross-drawing-type analysis of CV methods for construction documents, proposing a unified taxonomy, presenting quantitative bibliometric statistics, and systematically evaluating how foundation models (SAM, DINOv2, CLIP, VLMs) transfer to the construction drawing domain.
Abstract: The construction industry generates millions of 2D technical drawings — architectural floor plans, structural details, MEP (mechanical, electrical, plumbing) layouts, P&ID process diagrams, and civil site plans — that encode critical project information in a visual format fundamentally different from natural images. Computer vision methods for interpreting these drawings have advanced rapidly, driven by deep learning breakthroughs in object detection, semantic segmentation, OCR, graph neural networks, and most recently vision-language models and foundation models like SAM and Grounding DINO. Yet despite this progress, the field remains fragmented: research communities working on floor plan recognition, P&ID digitization, and structural drawing analysis operate largely in isolation, with no unified survey mapping the landscape. This paper presents the first comprehensive survey of computer vision methods for construction drawing understanding, covering 300+ papers spanning all major drawing types and CV methodologies. We propose a two-dimensional taxonomy organizing work by drawing type (architectural, structural, MEP, P&ID, civil) and CV task (symbol detection, layout segmentation, text recognition, table extraction, topology/graph reasoning). We provide extensive bibliometric analysis including publication trends from 2015 to 2026, venue distributions, method evolution from CNNs through transformers to foundation models, and geographic research activity. We compile unified benchmark comparison tables across public datasets including FloorplanCAD, CVC-FP, SESYD, DSSE-200, and emerging P&ID benchmarks. We analyze how foundation models and vision-language models are entering this domain and identify where they succeed and fail compared to domain-specific approaches. Finally, we outline open challenges — high-resolution processing, few-shot symbol detection, cross-drawing-type transfer, and the scarcity of annotated datasets — and propose concrete future research directions. This survey targets publication at TPAMI and aims to serve as the definitive reference for researchers and practitioners working at the intersection of computer vision and construction document intelligence.
Experiments: 1. **Paper Collection via Semantic Scholar API**: Use the Semantic Scholar API to systematically collect 300+ papers on construction drawing computer vision. You MUST make real HTTP calls to the Semantic Scholar API (https://api.semanticscholar.org/graph/v1/paper/search). Do NOT generate synthetic/fake paper data. Use time.sleep(1) between requests to respect rate limits. Query terms should include: 'floor plan recognition', 'floor plan segmentation', 'architectural drawing detection', 'P&ID symbol detection', 'piping and instrumentation diagram', 'construction drawing OCR', 'blueprint analysis', 'engineering drawing recognition', 'MEP drawing detection', 'structural drawing analysis', 'technical drawing understanding', 'building plan segmentation', 'CAD drawing recognition', 'construction document AI', 'symbol detection engineering drawings'. Store results in a structured JSON database with fields: title, authors, year, venue, abstract, citation count, DOI, and Semantic Scholar paper ID.

2. **Paper Categorization and Taxonomy Assignment**: For each collected paper, categorize along two dimensions: (a) drawing type — one of {floor_plan, structural, MEP, P&ID, civil, general_engineering, multi_type}, and (b) primary CV method — one of {cnn_detection, transformer_detection, segmentation, ocr_text, graph_reasoning, vlm_foundation, classical_cv, hybrid, dataset_benchmark}. Use the paper's title and abstract for classification. Store categorization results alongside the paper metadata. Generate a cross-tabulation matrix (drawing type x CV method) showing paper counts.

3. **Bibliometric Statistics and Trend Charts**: Generate the following statistical visualizations using matplotlib/seaborn from the REAL papers collected via the Semantic Scholar API in Experiment 1 — do NOT generate charts from simulated or fabricated data: (a) papers per year bar chart from 2015 to 2026, (b) stacked area chart showing method evolution over time (classical CV → CNN → Transformer → Foundation Model), (c) bar chart of paper counts by drawing type, (d) venue distribution chart (top 20 venues by paper count), (e) citation distribution analysis showing the most influential papers per sub-area, (f) geographic distribution of first-author affiliations. Save all charts as publication-quality PDF figures.

4. **Dataset and Benchmark Comparison Tables**: Compile a comprehensive table of all publicly available construction drawing datasets. Search for actual dataset papers via the Semantic Scholar API and extract real reported metrics (mAP, IoU, F1) from their abstracts and metadata. Do NOT fabricate benchmark numbers — only include metrics that are explicitly reported in collected papers. For each dataset record: name, drawing type, number of images, annotation type (bounding box, segmentation mask, graph, etc.), number of classes, image resolution, public availability (URL), and year released. Include at minimum: FloorplanCAD, CVC-FP, ROBIN, SESYD, R2V, DSSE-200, Raster-to-Vector, BRIDGE, ArchCAD-400K, and any P&ID benchmarks. Generate a second table comparing reported method performance (mAP, IoU, F1) across papers evaluated on the same datasets.

5. **Foundation Model Performance Analysis**: Collect and tabulate results from papers that evaluate foundation models (SAM, Grounding DINO, CLIP, GPT-4V/o, Qwen-VL, InternVL) on construction drawing tasks. Where available, compare zero-shot vs. fine-tuned performance against domain-specific baselines. Include results from benchmarks like AECV-Bench, CEQuest, and DesignQA if available. Generate a comparison chart showing foundation model vs. specialist model performance gaps across different drawing types.

6. **Lightweight Benchmark Experiments (Optional)**: If time and compute permit, run representative detection models (YOLOv8, RT-DETR, Grounding DINO) on publicly available construction drawing datasets (FloorplanCAD symbol detection, a P&ID dataset) to fill comparison gaps where no head-to-head results exist in the literature. Use AWS g5.2xlarge spot instances. Report mAP@50, mAP@50:95, and inference time. This provides original experimental contribution beyond pure literature review.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Coverage gaps are inevitable: some construction drawing sub-areas (e.g., structural detail drawings, shop drawings) have very few published papers, making comprehensive coverage difficult.

Non-English literature (particularly Chinese, Korean, and Japanese research on construction drawing analysis) may be underrepresented due to language barriers and indexing limitations in Semantic Scholar.
Many construction drawing datasets are proprietary or restricted to specific research groups, making it impossible to verify reported results or run independent benchmarks.
Paper categorization by drawing type and CV method relies on automated classification from titles and abstracts, which may introduce misclassification errors for papers that span multiple categories.

The field is evolving rapidly with foundation models; papers published during the survey writing period may not be captured, and the foundation model landscape may shift significantly before publication.

Bibliometric statistics from Semantic Scholar may not capture all relevant papers, particularly those published in construction/AEC-domain venues (e.g., Automation in Construction, ASCE journals) that may have lower coverage in CS-oriented databases.

The optional benchmark experiments (Type B) depend on compute availability and dataset access; if not completed, the survey relies entirely on reported results from other papers, which may use inconsistent evaluation protocols.
